issue.issue_text: whether a fundamental right under Article 19 or 21 can be claimed against anyone other than the State or its instrumentalities

law.law_name: Article 19 of the Constitution of India
law.description: Guarantees certain fundamental rights related to freedom of speech and expression, assembly, association, movement, residence, and profession.

law.law_name: Article 21 of the Constitution of India
law.description: Guarantees the right to life and personal liberty.

application.step: The Court first acknowledged that its original interpretation was that these fundamental rights could only be enforced against the State.
evidence: The original thinking of this Court that these rights can be enforced only against the State, changed over a period of time.

application.step: It then explained that this interpretation has evolved significantly over time. The scope of entities against whom these rights can be enforced has expanded.
evidence: The transformation was from “State” to “Authorities” to “instrumentalities of State” to “agency of the Government” to “impregnation with Governmental character” to “enjoyment of monopoly status conferred by State” to “deep and pervasive control” to the “nature of the duties/functions performed”.

application.step: Based on this judicial evolution, the majority concluded that these rights are indeed enforceable against non-State actors.
evidence: Therefore “A fundamental right under Article 19/21 can be enforced even against persons other than the State or its instrumentalities “.

application.step: A separate concurring opinion (by Justice B.V. Nagarathna) offered a more nuanced view. It held that while rights similar to those in Articles 19 and 21 operate horizontally (between private individuals) under common law, they are generally not directly justiciable as fundamental rights in Constitutional Courts against private parties, unless a statute recognizes them as such. An exception was made for the writ of Habeas Corpus under Article 21, which can be sought against a private person.
evidence: Held (per B.V. Nagarathna, J.): The rights in the realm of common law, which may be similar or identical in their content to the Fundamental Rights under Article 19/21, operate horizontally – However, the Fundamental Rights under Arts. 19 and 21, may not be justiciable horizontally before the Constitutional Courts except those rights which have been statutorily recognised... But a remedy in the form of writ of Habeas Corpus, if sought against a private person on the basis of Article 21 can be before a Constitutional Court

reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court, by a majority, decided that a fundamental right under Article 19 or 21 can be enforced even against persons and entities other than the State or its instrumentalities. This decision was based on the Court's evolving interpretation, which has progressively broadened the category of entities that can be held accountable for violating these rights.

ratio_decidendi.ratio: A right recognized and embodied in the Constitution can have a separate existence apart from the Constitution, such as in common law. In order to give effect to a constitutional right, a court must apply, or if necessary develop, the common law to the extent that legislation does not give effect to that right.
obiter: Law emerges as a norm limiting the application of power by the government over the citizen or by citizens over their fellows.
Theoretically all men are equal before the law and are equally bound by it regardless of their status, class, office or authority.
While the law enforces duties it also protects rights, even against the sovereign.
The principle of protecting rights applies with more vigour when the life and liberty of individuals is involved.
States have constitutional obligations to comfort and nurture the sustenance of the fundamental rights of citizens.

judicial_reasoning.core_finding: The court's reasoning is grounded in the concepts of constitutional fraternity and fundamental duty, which are identified as core constitutional values. The court holds that these principles establish a constitutional norm of respecting the dignity of others. This implies a 'constitutional assurance of mutual respect and concern for each other’s dignity,' which extends the application of fundamental rights beyond the State to interactions between individuals.
legal_tests_applied: The court applied a principle of holistic constitutional interpretation, using foundational values such as 'constitutional fraternity' and 'fundamental duty' to determine the scope and horizontal application of fundamental rights under Articles 19 and 21.
policy_considerations: Respect for the dignity of another is a constitutional norm.
Constitutional fraternity and the intrinsic value inhered in fundamental duty proclaim the constitutional assurance of mutual respect and concern for each other’s dignity.
The individual interest of each individual serves the collective interest and correspondingly the collective interest enhances the individual excellence.
